recommendations.regimenLabel: Resuscitate with balanced crystalloid / blood + control the source
steps: Two large-bore IV lines; rapid balanced crystalloid resuscitation.
Haemorrhagic: activate major haemorrhage protocol — transfuse blood/products, tranexamic acid early.
Identify and control the source (surgery, endoscopy, IR, compression).
Titrate to perfusion (MAP, urine output, lactate clearance) — avoid over-resuscitation in active bleeding.
Keep warm; correct coagulopathy and calcium.

drugRefs.why: Restores intravascular volume and perfusion; balanced crystalloid is preferred. Avoid over-resuscitation in active bleeding (permissive hypotension until source controlled).

drugRefs.dose: transfuse to restore oxygen-carrying capacity; give in balanced ratio with FFP/platelets per MHP
drugRefs.freq: guided by ongoing loss and haemodynamics
drugRefs.why: Definitive replacement in haemorrhagic shock; crystalloid alone is inadequate for significant blood loss.

refs: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22e — Approach to the Patient with Shock (Ch. 314)
European Guideline on Management of Major Bleeding and Coagulopathy Following Trauma

drugRefs.dose: 1 g IV over 10 min, then 1 g IV over 8 hours
drugRefs.why: Reduces mortality in traumatic haemorrhage when given early (within 3 h of injury).

drugRefs.dose: 10 mL of 10% (6.8 mmol Ca²⁺), guided by ionised calcium
drugRefs.why: Massive transfusion and citrate load cause hypocalcaemia, which worsens coagulopathy and cardiac contractility.

refs: CRASH-2 Trial — Tranexamic Acid in Trauma Haemorrhage
European Guideline on Management of Major Bleeding and Coagulopathy Following Trauma

confirm: Hypotension, tachycardia, cool peripheries, low JVP with a source of fluid/blood loss.
